kumis.name: Kumis
kumis.summary: Traditional fermented drink made from mare's milk, central to Turkic and Mongolic peoples of the Central and East Asian steppes, also called airag, with a higher alcohol content than kefir.

yakuts.name: Yakuts
yakuts.summary: A Turkic ethnic group, also called Sakha, native to North Siberia's Sakha Republic, who speak the Yakut language.

tandoor.name: Tandoor
tandoor.summary: Large vase-shaped clay oven, used since antiquity across South Asia, Western Asia, Central Asia and the Horn of Africa to bake flatbreads and roast meat at temperatures up to 480°C.

samsa-food.name: Samsa
samsa-food.summary: A savoury Central Asian pastry, typically a bun stuffed with meat and baked in a clay tandoor oven.

manti-food.name: Manti
manti-food.summary: A dumpling dish of spiced meat wrapped in dough, found across Central Asia, West Asia, the South Caucasus and the Balkans, and especially popular in Turkish cuisine.

samanu.name: Sumalak
samanu.summary: Another regional name for samanu, a sweet paste of germinated wheat and flour traditionally prepared for Nowruz, a practice traced back to the pre-Islamic Sasanian Persian Empire.

beshbarmak.name: Beshbarmak
beshbarmak.summary: Traditional Central Asian dish of boiled meat, noodles and onion broth, whose name means "five fingers" for the practice of eating it by hand.

bamyan.name: Bamyan
bamyan.summary: A city in central Afghanistan and capital of Bamyan Province, marking the most westerly point of Buddhist expansion and a trade hub blending Greek, Turkic, Persian, Chinese and Indian influences.

samanid-empire.name: Samanid dynasty
samanid-empire.summary: A Persianate Sunni Muslim dynasty that ruled an empire centered on Khorasan and Transoxiana from 819 to 999, patronizing Persian arts and scholars such as Rudaki and Avicenna.

khorasan.name: Khorasan
khorasan.summary: A historical region of the Iranian Plateau spanning parts of modern Afghanistan, Iran and Central Asia, with boundaries that varied over time and roots reaching back to Bronze Age complex societies there.

transoxiana.name: Transoxiana
transoxiana.summary: A Central Asian region beyond the Amu Darya river, named by Alexander the Great's troops in the 4th century BCE and later a Persian Achaemenid province called Sogdia.

buddhas-of-bamiyan.name: Buddhas of Bamiyan
buddhas-of-bamiyan.summary: Two monumental Buddhist statues carved into a cliff in Afghanistan's Bamiyan Valley, likely in the 6th to 7th century CE, and destroyed by the Taliban in March 2001.

northern-and-southern-dynasties.name: Northern dynasties
northern-and-southern-dynasties.summary: Term for the regimes ruling northern China during the 420–589 AD Northern and Southern dynasties period, a time of political division alongside flourishing arts, technology and the spread of Buddhism and Daoism.

xianbei.name: Xianbei
xianbei.summary: A nomadic, multi-ethnic confederation on the eastern Eurasian steppe descended from the Donghu, who rose to dominate the Mongolian Plateau after replacing the Xiongnu.

sogdia.name: Sogdia
sogdia.summary: An ancient Iranian civilisation between the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers, conquered in turn by Persian, Greek and other empires; its merchants were key middlemen on the Silk Road.

northern-wei.name: Northern Wei
northern-wei.summary: Imperial Chinese dynasty ruled by the Tuoba clan of the Xianbei, ruling northern China from 386 to 535 AD; noted for unifying northern China in 439 and firmly establishing Buddhism.

merv.name: Merv
merv.summary: A major ancient Iranian city in Central Asia on the Silk Road, settled from the 3rd millennium BC, that at times served as capital of the caliphate and of the Great Seljuk Empire and became a center of Islamic science.

sasanian-empire.name: Sasanian Empire
sasanian-empire.summary: An Iranian empire ruled by the House of Sasan from 224 to 651 AD, founded by Ardashir I to revive the legacy of the Achaemenid Empire; at its height it stretched from Egypt to Central Asia.

sogdian-art.name: Sogdian art
sogdian-art.summary: The visual art of the Sogdians, an Iranian people of Central Asia, flourishing from the 5th to 9th centuries and known especially for narrative painting and metalwork.

iwan.name: Iwan
iwan.summary: A rectangular, usually vaulted hall walled on three sides with one end open, a form of pre-Islamic Iranian origin that became common in Islamic architecture.

northern-qi.name: Northern Qi
northern-qi.summary: Chinese imperial dynasty that ruled the eastern part of northern China from 550 to 577 AD, founded by Gao Yang and eventually conquered by the Northern Zhou dynasty.

northern-zhou.name: Northern Zhou
northern-zhou.summary: Xianbei-led Chinese dynasty founded by the Yuwen clan, lasting from 557 to 581 AD, succeeding the Western Wei dynasty and overthrown by the Sui dynasty.

muqarnas.name: Muqarnas
muqarnas.summary: A three-dimensional, tiered niche-like decoration in Islamic architecture, likely developed in 11th-century Iraq, used to transition from walls to domes and vaults.

squinch.name: Squinch
squinch.summary: An architectural element that supports a round or octagonal dome on a square base, originating in Sassanid Persia and later used in Islamic, Georgian and Armenian buildings.

samarra.name: Samarra
samarra.summary: A city on the Tigris in Iraq, founded in 836 CE by the Abbasid caliph al-Mu'tasim as a new capital and military base; its ruins are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

hypostyle.name: Hypostyle
hypostyle.summary: An architectural hall whose roof is supported by columns.

caravanserai.name: Caravanserai
caravanserai.summary: A roadside or urban inn common across the Islamic world that sheltered travelers, merchants and pack animals along trade routes such as the Silk Road.

battle-of-talas.name: Battle of Talas
battle-of-talas.summary: A 751 battle in which the Abbasid Caliphate and its Karluk allies defeated the Tang dynasty's army for control of Central Asia, ending Tang westward expansion; Chinese prisoners taken there are said to have introduced papermaking to West Asia.

ordos-desert.name: Ordos Desert
ordos-desert.summary: A desert and steppe region of about 90,650 km² in Northwest China, made up of the Kubuqi and Mu Us deserts, with soil poorly suited to farming.

uyghur-khaganate.name: Uyghur Khaganate
uyghur-khaganate.summary: A Turkic tribal confederation empire that existed from the mid-8th to 9th centuries, which adopted Manichaeism as its official religion until its collapse in 830.

ordu-baliq.name: Ordu-Baliq
ordu-baliq.summary: Capital of the Uyghur Khaganate, built on the site of an earlier Göktürk capital; its ruins are now part of a UNESCO World Heritage site.

liang-shidu.name: Liang Shidu
liang-shidu.summary: Rebel who claimed the title of Emperor of China (517–628) and held the Ordos region for over a decade during the Sui-Tang transition before his defeat.

saka-language.name: Saka language
saka-language.summary: A Middle Eastern Iranian language attested in ancient Buddhist kingdoms of the western Tarim Basin, including Khotan, in documents dated from the 4th to the 11th century.

kingdom-of-khotan.name: Kingdom of Khotan
kingdom-of-khotan.summary: An ancient Buddhist Saka kingdom on the Silk Road's southern route through the Tarim Basin, known for silk, jade and carpets, existing over a thousand years until conquered by the Kara-Khanid Khanate in 1006.

orkhon-inscriptions.name: Orkhon Inscriptions
orkhon-inscriptions.summary: Bilingual 8th-century memorial steles in Middle Chinese and Old Turkic, erected by the Göktürks to honor Turkic princes Kul Tigin and Bilge Qaghan.

g-kt-rks.name: Göktürks
g-kt-rks.summary: A Turkic people of medieval Inner Asia who, under Bumin Qaghan and his sons, overthrew the Rouran Khaganate and founded the First Turkic Khaganate in the 6th century.

kul-tigin.name: Kul Tigin
kul-tigin.summary: General and prince of the Second Turkic Khaganate (684–731), honored with his brother Bilge Qaghan in the Orkhon inscriptions.

bilge-qaghan.name: Bilge Qaghan
bilge-qaghan.summary: The fourth qaghan of the Second Turkic Khaganate, who lived 683–734 CE; his achievements were recorded in the Orkhon inscriptions.

ilterish-qaghan.name: Ilterish Qaghan
ilterish-qaghan.summary: Founder of the Second Turkic Khaganate, reigning from 682 until his death in 691.

old-turkic-script.name: Old Turkic script
old-turkic-script.summary: An alphabet, also called Göktürk or Orkhon script, used by the Göktürks and other Turkic khanates from the 8th to 10th centuries, named after inscriptions found in Mongolia's Orkhon Valley.

sogdian-alphabet.name: Sogdian alphabet
sogdian-alphabet.summary: The script originally used to write the Sogdian language across Central Asia from about 100 to 1200 AD, later influencing the Old Turkic and Old Uyghur scripts.

first-turkic-khaganate.name: First Turkic Khaganate
first-turkic-khaganate.summary: A Turkic empire founded around 552 CE by the Ashina clan of the Göktürks, stretching from Manchuria to the Black Sea before splitting into eastern and western halves in 603.

ashina-tribe.name: Ashina clan
ashina-tribe.summary: A Turkic lineage that formed the ruling dynasty of the Goturks, rising to power in the mid-6th century after a revolt against the Rouran Khaganate.

oghuz-turks.name: Oghuz Turks
oghuz-turks.summary: A western Turkic people whose 8th-century tribal confederation in Central Asia became the ancestors of today's Turkmen, Azerbaijanis and Turks.

book-of-dede-korkut.name: Book of Dede Korkut
book-of-dede-korkut.summary: The most famous of the epic dastans of the Oghuz Turks, carrying the values of nomadic Turkic pre-Islamic life and surviving today in only a few manuscripts.

irk-bitig.name: Irk Bitig
irk-bitig.summary: A 9th-century Old Turkic manuscript on divination discovered in the Mogao Caves at Dunhuang in 1907, the only known complete text written in the Old Turkic script and a key source on early Turkic mythology.

mogao-caves.name: Mogao Caves
mogao-caves.summary: A system of about 500 Buddhist temple caves near Dunhuang, China, first dug in 366 CE and holding some of the finest Buddhist art made over 1,000 years; a hidden manuscript library was found there in 1900.

dunhuang.name: Dunhuang
dunhuang.summary: Oasis city in northwestern China and major Silk Road stop, known for the nearby Mogao Caves and its position at the entrance to the Hexi Corridor.

aurel-stein.name: Aurel Stein
aurel-stein.summary: Hungarian-born British archaeologist (1862–1943) known for explorations in Central Asia and for his collection of manuscripts from the Dunhuang caves.

old-uyghur-script.name: Old Uyghur script
old-uyghur-script.summary: A Turkic script adapted from the Aramaic alphabet, used for Buddhist, Manichaean and Christian texts in Turpan and Gansu from the 8th to 17th centuries, and ancestor of the Mongolian and Manchu alphabets.

turpan.name: Turpan
turpan.summary: A prefecture-level city in Xinjiang, China, with a population of about 694,000, whose historical center shifted over time from Yar-Khoto to Qocho and finally to Turpan itself.

tonyukuk.name: Tonyukuk
tonyukuk.summary: Supreme commander and adviser to four Göktürk khagans in the 7th–8th centuries, who led campaigns against steppe peoples and the Tang dynasty.

second-turkic-khaganate.name: Second Turkic Khaganate
second-turkic-khaganate.summary: A khaganate in Central and Eastern Asia founded by Ilterish of the Ashina clan of the Göktürks, lasting from 682 to 744 and centered on Ötüken.

mani-prophet.name: Mani
mani-prophet.summary: An Iranian prophet (c. 216–274 CE) who founded Manichaeism, born near Ctesiphon in the Parthian Empire and later imprisoned and killed under the Sasanian ruler Bahram I.

sogdian-language.name: Sogdian language
sogdian-language.summary: An Eastern Iranian language spoken in ancient Sogdia and by Sogdian communities in China; it served as a major lingua franca of Inner Asia and the First Turkic Khanate.

orkhon-valley.name: Orkhon Valley
orkhon-valley.summary: A UNESCO World Heritage landscape along the Orkhon River in central Mongolia, reflecting over two millennia of nomadic pastoral tradition.

tengri.name: Tengri
tengri.summary: The sky god of traditional Turkic and Mongolic beliefs, seen as eternal, supreme, and the judge and source of life; worship centered on him is called Tengrism.

tengrism.name: Tengrism
tengrism.summary: A belief system from the Eurasian steppes based on shamanism and animism and centered on the sky god Tengri, once the state religion of several medieval Turkic and Mongol states.

old-uyghur.name: Old Uyghur
old-uyghur.summary: A Turkic language spoken in the kingdom of Qocho from the 9th to 14th centuries, as well as in Gansu.

talas-river.name: Talas River
talas-river.summary: A river rising in Kyrgyzstan and flowing into Kazakhstan, 661 kilometres long, near which Tang and Abbasid forces clashed in 751.

syr-darya.name: Syr Darya
syr-darya.summary: A 2,256-kilometre river in Central Asia, historically called the Jaxartes, flowing from Kyrgyzstan through Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan toward the Aral Sea.

samarkand.name: Samarkand
samarkand.summary: A major city in southeastern Uzbekistan and one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in Central Asia, a key Silk Road center once capital of the Achaemenid satrapy of Sogdiana.

ptolemy.name: Ptolemy
ptolemy.summary: A Greco-Roman scholar of the 2nd century AD who wrote influential works on astronomy, geography and astrology; his geocentric model of the universe, promoted by the Catholic Church, was studied for over a thousand years.

almagest.name: Almagest
almagest.summary: Ptolemy's 2nd-century astronomical treatise that established the geocentric model of the universe, accepted for over 1,200 years.

al-biruni.name: Al-Biruni
al-biruni.summary: Iranian polymath of the Islamic Golden Age (c. 973-1050) who served the Ghaznavids as a historian and court astrologer and wrote a landmark work on India around 1030.

khwarazm.name: Khwarazm
khwarazm.summary: A large oasis region on the Amu Darya river delta in Central Asia, center of the Iranian Khwarezmian civilization until Turkic tribes took over in the 9th century.

xuan-paper.name: Xuan paper
xuan-paper.summary: Soft, fine-textured paper from ancient China, used for writing and painting. It is prized for Chinese calligraphy and painting.

al-ma-mun.name: Al-Ma'mun
al-ma-mun.summary: Seventh Abbasid caliph (786-833) who promoted the translation movement and flowering of science in Baghdad, during whose reign al-Khwarizmi's algebra text was published.

meridian-arc.name: Meridian arc
meridian-arc.summary: In geodesy and navigation, the curve between two points near the Earth's surface that share the same longitude, or the length of that curve.

al-farabi.name: Al-Farabi
al-farabi.summary: Early Islamic philosopher and music theorist (c. 870–950), called the "Second Master" after Aristotle. He is credited as the first Muslim to present philosophy as a coherent system and is known in the Latin West as Alpharabius.

otrar.name: Otrar
otrar.summary: Ancient city in southern Kazakhstan on the Silk Road, also called Farab. It was the center of a great oasis and linked Kazakhstan with China, Europe, the Middle East and Siberia.

burnishing-metal.name: Burnishing
burnishing-metal.summary: Smoothing and shining a surface by sliding another object against it hard enough to deform the surface. It is used on purpose in metalworking and manufacturing.

christopher-columbus.name: Christopher Columbus
christopher-columbus.summary: Italian explorer and navigator (1451–1506) whose four Spanish-sponsored voyages opened the way for European exploration and colonization of the Americas.

hephthalites.name: Hephthalites
hephthalites.summary: Central Asian people, also called the White Huns, who built an empire from about 450 CE and were militarily dominant until defeated by Turkic and Sasanian forces in 560.

eurasian-steppe.name: Eurasian Steppe
eurasian-steppe.summary: A grassland stretching about 8,000 km from Manchuria to Hungary that has been the main overland route between Eastern Europe, North Asia, Central Asia and East Asia since the Paleolithic, home to many nomadic empires.

seljuk-dynasty.name: Seljuk dynasty
seljuk-dynasty.summary: The Oghuz Turkic, Sunni Muslim ruling family, also called the House of Seljuk, that founded the Seljuk Empire along with the Sultanates of Kermân and Rum, targets of the First Crusade.

qiniq-tribe.name: Kınık
qiniq-tribe.summary: Oghuz Turkic tribe that lived north of the Caspian and Aral Seas in the 10th century; the House of Seljuk was a branch of this tribe.

oghuz-yabgu-state.name: Oghuz Yabgu State
oghuz-yabgu-state.summary: A Turkic state founded by the Oghuz Turks in 750, spanning territory between the Caspian and Aral Seas in what is now Kazakhstan.

illig-qaghan.name: Illig Qaghan
illig-qaghan.summary: Last qaghan of the Eastern Turkic Khaganate, who died on 13 February 634.

eastern-turkic-khaganate.name: Eastern Turkic Khaganate
eastern-turkic-khaganate.summary: A Turkic khaganate formed in the early 600s CE when the First Turkic Khaganate split in two, later defeated and absorbed by China's Tang dynasty.

tibetan-empire.name: Tibetan Empire
tibetan-empire.summary: An empire centered on the Tibetan Plateau, formed in the 7th century under Songtsen Gampo and later stretching from China to Afghanistan and India.

r-vaka.name: Śrāvaka
r-vaka.summary: A Sanskrit and Pali term meaning 'hearer' or 'disciple,' used in both Buddhism and Jainism; in Jainism it can mean any lay follower, and in Buddhism sometimes a distinguished disciple of the Buddha.

r-vakay-na.name: Śrāvakayāna
r-vakay-na.summary: One of three paths recognized in Indian Buddhism, describing enlightenment reached by listening to a fully awakened Buddha's teachings in order to become an Arhat.

yijing-monk.name: Yijing
yijing-monk.summary: Tang-era Chinese Buddhist monk (635–713 CE) and travel writer whose account is a key source on medieval Srivijaya and Gupta-era India; he also translated Buddhist texts from Sanskrit.

mah-saka.name: Mahisasaka
mah-saka.summary: One of the early Buddhist schools, possibly originating from a dispute at the Second Buddhist Council, from which the Dharmaguptaka sect later branched.

dharmaguptaka.name: Dharmaguptaka
dharmaguptaka.summary: One of the early Buddhist schools, influential in early Central Asian and Chinese Buddhism, whose monastic rules are still followed across East Asia today.

k-yap-ya.name: Kāśyapīya
k-yap-ya.summary: One of the early Buddhist schools in India.

sarvastivada.name: Sarvastivada
sarvastivada.summary: An early Buddhist school established around Ashoka's reign in the 3rd century BC, teaching that phenomena exist across past, present and future; influential in North India and Central Asia until the 7th century CE.

ghaznavid-empire.name: Ghaznavid Empire
ghaznavid-empire.summary: Persianate Muslim empire of Turkic origin that flourished from 977 to 1186, stretching at its height from the Oxus River to the Indus Valley.

bactria.name: Bactria
bactria.summary: An ancient Iranian region of Central Asia between the Oxus River and the Hindu Kush, an early centre of Zoroastrianism later ruled by the Achaemenid Empire and conquered by Alexander the Great.

naw-bahar.name: Nava Vihara
naw-bahar.summary: Buddhist monasteries near ancient Balkh in northern Afghanistan, an important center of Buddhist learning from the 7th to 11th centuries CE, sometimes called the 'Nalanda of Central Asia'.

xuanzang.name: Xuanzang
xuanzang.summary: 7th-century Chinese Buddhist monk and traveler (602–664) whose journey to India in 629–645 brought hundreds of Buddhist texts back to China for translation.

balkh.name: Balkh
balkh.summary: A city in northern Afghanistan, historically a center of Zoroastrianism and Buddhism known to Persians as Zariaspa and Greeks as Bactra; capital of ancient Bactria, later devastated by the Mongols.

old-book-of-tang.name: Old Book of Tang
old-book-of-tang.summary: The first classic historical work on the Tang dynasty, 200 chapters compiled in the 10th century, one of China's Twenty-Four Histories.

shiwei-people.name: Shiwei people
shiwei-people.summary: A Mongolic people of far-eastern Mongolia, northern Inner Mongolia and Manchuria, recorded from the Northern Wei period until Genghis Khan's rise in 1206, considered ancestors of the Mongols.
